title: Anyonic Neural Network Wavefunctions
authors: Andres Perez Fadon, Pok Man Tam, Leyna Shackleton
abstract: The macroscopic behavior of a non-interacting gas of Abelian anyons has remained unsettled for many decades. Prior numerical methods employing exact diagonalization in the continuum and on the plane have been limited to small system sizes, at most $N = 4$ anyons. Using the rapidly developing technology of neural network wavefunctions, we develop variational ansatze appropriate for studying continuum models of the Abelian anyon gas. The neural network architecture, which we call "AnyNet", is capable of exactly enforcing the non-analytic short-distance behavior induced by the anyonic statistics. We demonstrate excellent agreement with exact diagonalization for $N=4$ anyons, obtain accurate results up to $N = 16$ for intermediate statistics, and study up to $N=20$ for almost-fermionic anyons, matching perturbative results within a 0.4% discrepancy. We use this methodology to study anyons in a harmonic trap, and anyonic atoms as a model for anyon binding to impurities. We study the structure of anyonic wavefunctions as the statistics parameter is varied. We focus on the single-particle density, the pair density, the angular momentum, and the scaling of the wavefunction as multiple anyons coalesce. This work opens doors to understanding the macroscopic behavior of anyons, for which rich phases have been predicted theoretically.
summary: This paper introduces 'AnyNet,' a novel neural network ansatz, to overcome the computational limitations in studying non-interacting Abelian anyon gases. By enforcing the required short-distance statistical behavior, the method achieves high accuracy for systems up to $N=20$. This opens the door to understanding the macroscopic quantum phases predicted for anyons in various physical traps.
main_problem: The core challenge is developing a robust numerical method to study the macroscopic behavior of non-interacting Abelian anyon gases, whose wavefunctions exhibit complex, non-analytic short-distance behavior.
main_result: The proposed 'AnyNet' neural network ansatz successfully enforces the required short-distance statistics, yielding accurate results up to $N=16$ and matching perturbative theory within 0.4% for $N=20$.
method: The authors employ Neural Network Variational Monte Carlo (NNVMC) using a specialized ansatz ('AnyNet') to parameterize the variational state, circumventing the difficulties associated with multi-valued anyon wavefunctions via a gauge transformation.
model_or_system: The system is a non-interacting gas of Abelian anyons in two dimensions, modeled by a Hamiltonian that is transformed into an effective fermionic gauge problem. The study is applied to anyons in a harmonic trap and as a model for impurity binding.
key_observables: Single-particle density, pair density, angular momentum, and the energy spectrum ($E$).
important_parameters: The exchange statistics parameter $\alpha$ ($0 \le \alpha \le 1$), the number of anyons $N$ (tested up to $N=20$), and the harmonic trap parameters.
main_assumptions: The method relies on mapping the anyon problem to an equivalent single-valued fermionic wavefunction via a statistical gauge transformation. Previous methods were limited to very small system sizes ($N \le 4$).
figures_summary: Figures schematically illustrate the statistical transmutation process and the structure of the AnyNet ansatz. Tables present detailed numerical data for energy, angular momentum, and radius expectation values across varying parameters.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical problem and the need for a new method. It details the gauge transformation and the AnyNet ansatz. Subsequently, it presents results comparing AnyNet against exact diagonalization and perturbation theory for various system sizes and statistics parameters, concluding with applications to traps and binding.
why_interesting: The development and successful application of AnyNet represent a significant methodological advance in quantum many-body physics, providing a powerful tool to simulate strongly correlated systems whose wavefunctions are analytically intractable.

FIG. 3. Schematic of the AnyNet network. We start by obtaining single-particle features, such as the position of the anyons, {ri}, and two-particle features, such as the relative displacements between pairs {ri −rj}. These features are then fed into the FermiNet architecture, from which the latent vectors hL i are obtained. The latent vectors are used to construct ordinary (bulk) orbitals, and the Vij and Sij tensors, which describe the shape of the wavefunction near anyon coincidences. The latent vectors are also pooled (averaged) and fed to a second small MLP, a method usually called Deep Set in machine learning.
